q: At point B on the displayed linear demand curve, what price and quantity are shown?
feedback: Point B is marked at P = $8 and Q = 60.

q: Which labeled point is the midpoint of the displayed linear demand curve?
feedback: The line runs from P = $16, Q = 0 to P = $0, Q = 120, so its midpoint is P = $8, Q = 60 at B.

q: Which labeled point lies in the inelastic portion of the displayed linear demand curve?
options: All three points are equally elastic
feedback: Below the midpoint of a linear demand curve, quantity is relatively large and price relatively small, so demand is inelastic; A is in that region.

q: At point C, price is $12 and quantity is 30. What total-revenue amount follows from those graph values?
feedback: At C, P = $12 and Q = 30, so total revenue is $12 × 30 = $360.

q: A seller is at point B, charging $8 and selling 60 units. What total revenue does that combination generate?
feedback: At B, P = $8 and Q = 60, so total revenue is $480.

q: Moving from C to B lowers price from $12 to $8 while total revenue rises from $360 to $480. What does that imply about demand over this interval?
options: Demand is unit elastic throughout the interval
feedback: When a price cut raises total revenue, demand is elastic over the interval.

q: Using the midpoint formula between C (P = $12, Q = 30) and B (P = $8, Q = 60), the absolute price elasticity of demand is approximately:
feedback: The percentage quantity change is 30/45 ≈ 66.7% and the percentage price change is 4/10 = 40%, giving elasticity about 1.67.

q: Using the midpoint formula between B (P = $8, Q = 60) and A (P = $4, Q = 90), the absolute price elasticity of demand is approximately:
feedback: The percentage quantity change is 30/75 = 40% and the percentage price change is 4/6 ≈ 66.7%, giving elasticity about 0.60.

q: Using the midpoint formula between C (P = $12, Q = 30) and A (P = $4, Q = 90), the absolute price elasticity of demand is:
feedback: From C to A, quantity changes by 60 around an average of 60 and price changes by 8 around an average of 8, so both percentage changes are 100%.

q: Why does elasticity change along the displayed linear demand curve even though the curve has constant slope?
options: The demand curve changes slope at B
The price-to-quantity ratio changes along the curve
feedback: For a linear demand curve, point elasticity depends on both the constant slope term and the changing P/Q ratio.

q: A seller moves from C to B on the displayed demand curve. Total revenue rises by $120 while price falls. Which conclusion follows?
options: Demand is perfectly inelastic over C–B
Demand must have elasticity of zero
feedback: A price decrease that raises total revenue signals elastic demand.

q: A seller moves from B to A on the displayed demand curve. Total revenue falls from $480 to $360 while price falls. Which conclusion follows?
options: Demand is perfectly elastic over B–A
Demand has constant unit elasticity over B–A
feedback: A price decrease that lowers total revenue signals inelastic demand.

q: Point B yields the largest total revenue among A, B, and C. What elasticity condition is associated with that midpoint of a linear demand curve?
feedback: On a linear demand curve, total revenue is maximized at the midpoint, where demand is unit elastic.

q: C→B and B→A each involve a $4 price change and a 30-unit quantity change. Why can the first interval be elastic while the second is inelastic?
options: The demand curve has different slopes in the two intervals
The percentage-change bases differ across the two intervals
Elasticity uses only the absolute quantity change
Elasticity is determined only by the direction of price
feedback: Elasticity depends on percentage changes, so identical absolute changes can produce different elasticities when the average price and quantity bases differ.

q: Starting from point A, which pricing move toward the midpoint raises total revenue on the displayed demand curve?
options: Cut price farther below point A
Raise price toward point C but skip B
Keep price fixed because revenue cannot change
feedback: At A, demand is inelastic. Moving toward B raises price from $4 to $8 while total revenue rises from $360 to $480.

q: At point C, the seller is on the elastic portion of demand. Which direction of price change moves revenue toward its maximum at B?
options: Raise price farther above point C
Lower price toward point A without passing B
Keep price fixed because C already maximizes revenue
feedback: At C, demand is elastic. Moving toward B lowers price and raises total revenue from $360 to $480.

q: Checkpoint: Which labeled point on the displayed linear demand curve represents unit elasticity and the maximum total revenue among A, B, and C?
feedback: B is the midpoint of the linear demand curve and yields the highest total revenue, so demand is unit elastic there.

q: Checkpoint: The displayed graph gives total revenues of $360 at C, $480 at B, and $360 at A. Which pattern is correct as price falls from C through B to A?
options: Revenue falls continuously because price falls
Revenue rises in the elastic region, peaks at unit elasticity, then falls in the inelastic region
Revenue is constant because slope is constant
Revenue peaks in the inelastic region and then rises
feedback: The total-revenue test tracks the shift from elastic demand above the midpoint to unit elasticity at B and inelastic demand below it.

q: At a price of $10 in the displayed graph, which curve shows the larger quantity demanded?
feedback: At P = $10, point B on D1 is Q = 45 while point D on D2 is Q = 35.

q: When price is $6, which demand curve shows the larger quantity demanded?
feedback: At P = $6, D1 is at point A with Q = 95, while D2 is at point C with Q = 55.

q: When price falls from $10 to $6 on D1, quantity demanded rises from 45 to 95. What is the quantity change?
feedback: The change is 95 − 45 = 50 units.

q: When price falls from $10 to $6 on D2, quantity demanded rises from 35 to 55. What is the quantity change?
feedback: The change is 55 − 35 = 20 units.

q: For the same price decrease from $10 to $6, which curve is more price elastic over the labeled interval?
options: Elasticity cannot be compared from the labeled points
feedback: D1 has the much larger proportional quantity response to the same proportional price change.

q: Using B (P = $10, Q = 45) and A (P = $6, Q = 95), the midpoint price elasticity of demand on D1 is approximately:
feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 50/70 ≈ 71.4% and the price change is 4/8 = 50%, so elasticity is about 1.43.

q: Using D (P = $10, Q = 35) and C (P = $6, Q = 55), the midpoint price elasticity of demand on D2 is approximately:
feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 20/45 ≈ 44.4% and the price change is 4/8 = 50%, so elasticity is about 0.89.

q: Using the labeled $10-to-$6 price change, which classification is correct?
options: Both D1 and D2 are elastic
D1 is elastic and D2 is inelastic
D1 is inelastic and D2 is elastic
Both D1 and D2 are unit elastic
feedback: The midpoint coefficients are about 1.43 for D1 and 0.89 for D2.

q: On D1, total revenue changes from $450 at B to $570 at A when price falls from $10 to $6. What does that confirm?
options: D1 is perfectly inelastic over B–A
D1 has zero elasticity over B–A
feedback: A price cut that increases total revenue indicates elastic demand.

q: On D2, total revenue changes from $350 at D to $330 at C when price falls from $10 to $6. What does that confirm?
options: D2 is perfectly elastic over D–C
D2 is unit elastic over D–C
feedback: A price cut that reduces total revenue indicates inelastic demand.

q: The midpoint elasticities over the labeled intervals are about 1.43 for D1 and 0.89 for D2. Which statement follows?
options: Only D1 is above the unit-elastic threshold
Only D2 is above the unit-elastic threshold
feedback: Elasticity above one is elastic; 1.43 exceeds one while 0.89 does not.

q: Suppose D1 and D2 describe similar goods, but one has many close substitutes and the other has few. Which assignment is most consistent with the displayed responses?
options: D2 has more close substitutes than D1
D1 has more close substitutes than D2
Both must have the same number of substitutes
feedback: More close substitutes make buyers more responsive to price changes, consistent with the larger response on D1.

q: In the displayed graph, horizontal D1 represents:
feedback: A horizontal demand curve is the limiting case of perfectly elastic demand.

q: In the displayed graph, vertical D2 represents:
feedback: A vertical demand curve means quantity demanded does not change when price changes.

q: Following D2 from point A at P = $5 to point B at P = $7, what happens to quantity demanded?
feedback: D2 is vertical at Q = 50, so the price change does not alter quantity demanded.

q: What is the price elasticity coefficient for the vertical D2 curve?
feedback: With zero percentage change in quantity despite a price change, the elasticity coefficient is zero.

q: On horizontal D1 at P = $5, what is the idealized implication of a seller attempting to charge a price above $5?
feedback: With perfectly elastic demand, buyers will not accept a price above the market price represented by the horizontal curve.

q: How do the absolute elasticity magnitudes of D1 and D2 compare?
options: D1 equals zero while D2 approaches infinity
D1 approaches infinity while D2 equals zero
feedback: Perfectly elastic demand is the infinite-elasticity limiting case; perfectly inelastic demand has elasticity zero.

q: Checkpoint: Which displayed demand curve has zero price elasticity?
feedback: D2 is vertical, so quantity does not respond to price and elasticity is zero.

q: Checkpoint: Moving from A to B along D2 raises price from $5 to $7 while quantity stays at 50. What does that demonstrate?
feedback: A vertical demand curve allows price to change with no quantity response, the definition of perfect inelasticity.

q: At a price of $8, what quantity is supplied on the short-run supply curve?
feedback: Point A on the short-run supply curve is Q = 70 at P = $8.

q: At a price of $8, which supply curve shows the larger quantity response from the common starting point at P = $4, Q = 60?
feedback: Long-run supply reaches Q = 100, compared with Q = 70 in the short run.

q: When price rises from $4 to $8, how much does quantity supplied rise in the short run?
feedback: Short-run quantity rises from 60 to 70, a 10-unit increase.

q: Why does the displayed long-run supply curve show a larger response to the same price increase?
options: Producers have less time to change output
Producers have more time to adjust capacity and inputs
Long-run quantity is fixed by definition
Price changes are smaller in the long run
feedback: More adjustment time usually allows firms to expand capacity, enter, switch inputs, and otherwise respond more strongly.

q: Using the midpoint formula from (P = $4, Q = 60) to point A (P = $8, Q = 70), short-run price elasticity of supply is approximately:
feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 10/65 ≈ 15.4% and the price change is 4/6 ≈ 66.7%, giving PES ≈ 0.23.

q: Using the midpoint formula from (P = $4, Q = 60) to point B (P = $8, Q = 100), long-run price elasticity of supply is approximately:
feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 40/80 = 50% and the price change is 4/6 ≈ 66.7%, giving PES ≈ 0.75.

q: A persistent price increase initially moves producers toward A but, after more adjustment time, toward B. Which elasticity principle does this illustrate?
options: Supply tends to become more elastic over longer time horizons
Supply must become perfectly inelastic over time
Short-run supply is always more elastic than long-run supply
Time horizon affects demand but never supply
feedback: The larger long-run quantity response illustrates that firms can adjust more fully when given time.

q: The midpoint PES values are about 0.23 in the short run and 0.75 in the long run. Approximately how many times larger is the long-run elasticity?
feedback: 0.75 ÷ 0.23 is about 3.25, confirming a substantially larger long-run response.

q: Checkpoint: Price rises from $4 to $8. Short-run quantity rises from 60 to 70 while long-run quantity rises from 60 to 100. Which curve is more elastic?
options: Elasticity cannot be compared from these changes
feedback: The long-run curve shows the larger proportional quantity response to the same proportional price change.

q: Checkpoint: Using the midpoint formula for the $4-to-$8 price increase, which approximate pair correctly compares supply elasticity?
feedback: The short-run response is about 0.23 and the long-run response about 0.75, so long-run supply is more elastic.
